result: Notch signaling components remain expressed in neural crest after induction, with variable levels of Notch activity between premigratory trunk neural crest cells.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by in situ hybridization data showing expression of Notch components (notch1a, dlb, dld, her4) in migrating neural crest cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and imaging data from the Notch reporter line 12xNRE:egfp showing variable GFP expression levels in premigratory TNC cells (Figure 1). The data directly demonstrate both continued expression and variability in Notch activity.

result: Notch inhibition impairs trunk neural crest induction up to 11 hpf, while cranial and vagal neural crest induction is independent of Notch signaling.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C4 are supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced or absent crestin expression in DAPT-treated embryos at different developmental stages (Figure 2D) and confirmation of previous work by Cornell and Eisen, 2000. The temporal specificity and population-specific effects are clearly demonstrated.

result: Notch inhibition at 12 hpf reduces trunk neural crest derivatives and migration, delaying rather than completely halting migration.
evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced expression of differentiation markers (mbp, bdh) and pigmentation (Figure 3A-F), reduced chain formation and ventral advance (Figure 3G-J), and time-course analysis showing new chain formation over time despite DAPT treatment (Figure 3K). The data demonstrate both the reduction in derivatives and the delay rather than complete block of migration.

result: Both genetic and chemical Notch inhibition produce similar migration defects, and both gain and loss of Notch function result in similar phenotypes, indicating that precise regulation of Notch signaling levels is required for trunk neural crest migration.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by quantification showing similar reduction in chain numbers for both chemical (DAPT) and genetic (hs:dnSu(H)) inhibition, as well as for both Notch GOF (hs:Gal4;UAS:NICD) and LOF conditions (Figure 3L). The paradoxical similarity of GOF and LOF phenotypes strongly supports the conclusion that intermediate Notch levels are required.

result: Under Notch inhibition, trunk neural crest leader cells are unable to retain the front position, show reduced ventral advance, and have decreased speed and directionality, while somite and neuron development remain unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by live imaging data showing leader overtaking events (Figure 4C, Figure 5B), reduced ventral distance (Figure 5C), and quantitative analysis showing reduced speed and directionality (Figure 5D-E). Control experiments showing normal somite and neuronal marker expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) rule out indirect effects through tissue environment.

result: Cell-autonomous inhibition of Notch signaling in neural crest phenocopies chemical inhibition, confirming that Notch activity is autonomously required for identity allocation and that loss of Notch signaling establishes a homogeneous follower population.
evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by live imaging data from Sox10:Kalt4;UAS:dnSu(H) embryos showing similar phenotypes to chemical inhibition (Figure 4D, Figure 5A-C) and quantitative analysis showing that leader cells adopt follower characteristics (Figure 5D-E). The cell-autonomous approach definitively demonstrates that Notch acts within neural crest cells rather than through environmental effects.

result: Notch overactivation leads to loss of group coherence and impaired ventral advance, with follower cells adopting leader characteristics including increased speed but reduced directionality.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by live imaging data from Notch GOF conditions (Sox10:Kalt4;UAS:NICD) showing loss of coherence and impaired advance (Figure 4F, Figure 5A-C), and quantitative analysis showing increased speed but reduced directionality (Figure 5D-E). The data demonstrate that all cells adopt leader-like behavior under Notch GOF.

result: Notch activity controls phox2bb expression and allocates trunk neural crest migratory identity, with high Notch levels leading to phox2bb expression and leader identity, while low Notch activity results in follower identity.
evaluation: Claims C20-C24 are supported by RNAscope data showing phox2bb expression predominantly in leader cells under control conditions (Figure 6A-B, G), in all cells under Notch GOF (Figure 6C-D, G), and absent under Notch inhibition (Figure 6E-G). The molecular marker data directly correlates with the behavioral observations and provides mechanistic insight.

result: Alterations of Notch signaling lead to homogeneous trunk neural crest populations unable to undergo collective migration, suggesting Notch lateral inhibition as the mechanism for migratory identity acquisition.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by the combined data showing that both Notch GOF and LOF produce homogeneous populations (all leaders or all followers) that cannot migrate collectively. However, C26 is somewhat speculative as direct evidence of lateral inhibition mechanism (e.g., ligand-receptor dynamics) is not provided, though the pattern is consistent with lateral inhibition.

result: Computational modeling demonstrates that cell heterogeneity is required for trunk neural crest migration, with optimal recapitulation of in vivo behavior achieved at 1:2 or 1:3 leader/follower ratios, and CIL intensity as the most important distinguishing parameter.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are supported by computational modeling results showing that homogeneous cell simulations cannot match in vivo behavior (Figure 7C), that 1:2 and 1:3 ratios best recapitulate control and Notch-altered conditions (Figure 4B, E, G, Figure 5), and that linear discriminant analysis identifies CIL intensity as the most important parameter (Figure 7F). The modeling provides quantitative predictions that are later validated experimentally.

result: Leader cells arise from asymmetric division of a single progenitor cell that produces a larger prospective leader and smaller follower, while other progenitors divide symmetrically to produce two follower cells.
evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by live imaging and tracking data showing asymmetric division producing cells of different sizes (102±20 vs 72±9 μm²) that adopt different identities (Figure 8A-B), and symmetric divisions producing similar-sized cells (87±27 μm²) that both become followers (Figure 8C-D). The data directly demonstrate the origin of size differences and identity allocation.

result: Leader and follower progenitors divide at different spatial locations and follow different temporal patterns, with leaders dividing during migration (86% M→D) at the NT/not boundary, while followers divide before migration (90% D→M) in the premigratory area, suggesting asynchronous cell cycle progression.
evaluation: Claims C36-C42 are supported by spatial analysis showing restricted anterior division of leader progenitors (Figure 8E), quantification of division patterns (Figure 8H), and position measurements (Figure 8I). The data demonstrate clear spatial and temporal differences in division patterns between leaders and followers, though the inference of asynchronous cell cycle progression (C42) requires additional validation provided in later claims.

result: Cell cycle inhibitors effectively block cell division without affecting neural crest induction, and inhibition of cell cycle progression results in reduced migration that is reversible upon drug withdrawal, demonstrating that active cell cycle progression is required for trunk neural crest migration.
evaluation: Claims C43-C49 are supported by quantification showing >90% inhibition of mitotic figures (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), normal crestin expression at 16 hpf (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-F), reduced chain numbers and ventral advance (Figure 9A-H), live imaging showing maintained motility but impaired ventral migration (Figure 9—video 1), and recovery after drug withdrawal (Figure 9G-H). The data demonstrate both the requirement for cell cycle progression and the specificity of the effect.

result: Leader cells initiate migration in S-phase (79%) while follower cells start movement during G1 (77%), demonstrating that cell cycle progression is required for migration and that leaders and followers initiate movement at different cell cycle points.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by analysis of Sox10:FUCCI embryos showing differential cell cycle phase at migration initiation (Figure 9I-J). The data directly demonstrate the correlation between cell cycle phase and migration initiation, though the causal relationship is inferred from the combined data with cell cycle inhibition experiments.

result: Leader and follower cells have similar total cell cycle length but differ markedly in G1 and S-phase duration, with leaders having short G1 (3.2±0.6 hr) and long S-phase (8.7±1.3 hr), while followers have long G1 (7.4±2.7 hr) and short S-phase (4.6±2.8 hr).
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by quantification using PCNA-GFP showing no significant difference in total cell cycle length (Figure 10B) but striking differences in G1 and S-phase lengths (Figure 10C-D). The data provide detailed characterization of cell cycle differences between leaders and followers, though the suggestion that this regulates migratory behavior (C57) is speculative.

result: Notch inhibition does not affect total cell cycle length or cell number but causes leader cells to adopt follower-like cell cycle progression (long G1, short S-phase) and abolishes size differences, demonstrating that Notch activity defines migratory identity by regulating cell cycle progression.
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by quantification showing no change in total cell cycle length (Figure 11A) or cell number (Figure 9—figure supplement 1I), but significant changes in G1 and S-phase lengths (Figure 11B) and cell area (Figure 11C-D) under Notch inhibition. The data demonstrate that Notch regulates cell cycle progression and that this correlates with identity changes.

result: Follower cells show a bimodal distribution of cell cycle phase lengths with 26-31% resembling leaders, fulfilling computational model predictions of 1:2 or 1:3 leader/follower ratios, and this bimodal distribution is lost upon Notch inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by quantification showing reduced standard deviation under Notch inhibition (Figure 11B), frequency distribution analysis showing bimodal distribution for followers with a subset resembling leaders (Figure 11E-F), and loss of bimodal distribution under Notch inhibition (Figure 11G-H). The data provide strong support for the computational model predictions and demonstrate heterogeneity within the follower population.

result: High-magnification analysis reveals phox2bb expression in the third follower cell in addition to leaders, supporting the conclusion that Notch activity allocates migratory identity by controlling cell cycle progression and that migratory chains are formed of one leader for every three followers.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by high-magnification RNAscope images showing phox2bb expression in the third follower cell (Figure 11I-N) and the combined data from Notch manipulation, cell cycle analysis, computational modeling, and phox2bb expression patterns. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports the 1:3 leader/follower ratio.

result: Prior work in chicken embryos and other systems demonstrates connections between cell cycle progression and migration, cell size and G1/S transition, cyclins and migration, Rac1 activity and cell cycle, CDKIs and motility, actin branching and G1/S transition, Notch and cell cycle regulation, cell cycle and Notch activity, and Notch/cell cycle effects on migration in cancer and angiogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C71-C82 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims provide context for the current findings and suggest potential molecular mechanisms, though they do not constitute new findings from this study. The citations appear appropriate and relevant to the discussion.
